goal: Predict multiplicative change, read doubling and half-life clocks, and distinguish ideal exponential growth from resource-limited reality.

lessons.objective: By the end you can work backward from a full bottle to its half-full and quarter-full times.

beats.text: Picture a tiny smiling bacterium beside a huge bottle.
If the bottle becomes full at noon and doubles every 20 minutes, when was it one-quarter full?
A bacterium doubles every 20 minutes in an idealized bottle that is full at noon. The bottle was only half full at 11:40.
11:20: two doubling intervals before noon. Run the film backward and a full bottle becomes half a bottle in just one generation.
Challenge this tempting claim: “Half full means half the total elapsed time has passed.” Use a clock jumping from 11:40 to noon to show what the model actually says.

Explain without the picture: What idealization makes the bottle puzzle exponential until the final instant? Check your reasoning against: Every bacterium keeps doubling every 20 minutes with no resource limitation before the capacity cutoff.

visuals.title: The last doubling fills the bottle
visuals.goal: Run the film backward and a full bottle becomes half a bottle in just one generation.

lessons.objective: By the end you can distinguish constant differences from constant ratios and predict a population.

beats.text: Picture rows of 1, 2, 4, 8 colored cells.
Starting with 3 cells and doubling every generation, how many are there after four generations?
Exponential growth multiplies by the same factor over equal time intervals. From 1 cell, five doublings produce 32 cells.
48 cells: 3 × 2^4. Each generation copies the entire crowd, so the amount added grows along with the crowd.
Challenge this tempting claim: “Doubling adds two individuals each step.” Use a staircase whose risers double in height to show what the model actually says.
Explain without the picture: Write the discrete growth formula for initial amount N0, per-step fractional growth r, and n steps. Check your reasoning against: N(n) = N0(1+r)^n.

visuals.title: Multiplication instead of addition
visuals.goal: Each generation copies the entire crowd, so the amount added grows along with the crowd.

lessons.objective: By the end you can calculate doubling times and count elapsed doublings.

beats.text: Picture equal horizontal gaps between heights 10, 20, 40.
A population starts at 50 and doubles every 3 hours; what is it after 12 hours?
For N(t)=N0 exp(kt), the doubling time is ln(2)/k. A constant doubling time means a constant proportional growth rate.
800: four doublings multiply 50 by 16. A doubling time counts how long it takes the entire graph to climb to twice its current height.
Challenge this tempting claim: “Doubling time becomes shorter just because there are more cells.” Use a ruler marked in generations rather than cells to show what the model actually says.
Explain without the picture: What is the doubling time for continuous rate k = 0.2 per hour? Check your reasoning against: ln(2)/0.2 ≈ 3.47 hours.

visuals.title: Doubling time is a clock
visuals.goal: A doubling time counts how long it takes the entire graph to climb to twice its current height.

lessons.objective: By the end you can compute compound balances and distinguish them from simple interest.

beats.text: Picture coins sprouting smaller coin trees.
Deposit 200 at 5% effective annual interest for two years, with no deposits or withdrawals. What is the balance?
Compounding applies each new percentage to principal plus accumulated interest. At 10% annually, 100 becomes 121 after two years.
220.50: 200 × 1.05^2. Interest is a new worker that starts earning interest of its own next year.
Challenge this tempting claim: “Ten percent for two years always gives exactly twenty percent total growth.” Use bars labeled 100, 110, and 121 to show what the model actually says.

Explain without the picture: How does simple interest differ from compound interest for a fixed initial principal? Check your reasoning against: Simple interest applies the percentage only to the initial principal; compound interest applies it to the current balance.

visuals.title: Interest earns interest
visuals.goal: Interest is a new worker that starts earning interest of its own next year.

lessons.objective: By the end you can translate between continuous rates and effective per-period multipliers.

beats.text: Picture a tangent arrow that lengthens with the curve height.
For N0=10 and continuous rate k=ln(2) per hour, what is N after three hours?
Continuous proportional growth satisfies dN/dt=kN and has solution N0 exp(kt). Its rate k is not the same as the effective per-period fractional increase.
80: exp(3 ln(2)) = 8. Zoom into a growth curve until each tiny rise is proportional to the height already there.
Challenge this tempting claim: “A continuous rate k=1 means only 100% total growth in one time unit.” Use compounding intervals shrinking toward a smooth curve to show what the model actually says.
Explain without the picture: What differential equation expresses continuous proportional growth? Check your reasoning against: dN/dt = kN.

visuals.title: Continuous growth and e
visuals.goal: Zoom into a growth curve until each tiny rise is proportional to the height already there.

lessons.objective: By the end you can interpret slope and spacing on a logarithmic population plot.

beats.text: Picture a ladder labeled 1, 10, 100, 1000.
On a base-10 log axis, are the distances from 10 to 100 and from 100 to 1000 equal?
On a logarithmic vertical axis, equal distances represent equal ratios. A positive exponential becomes a straight line whose slope encodes its growth rate.
Yes; both represent multiplication by 10 and a log10 increase of 1. A log axis folds each doubling into the same visual step, however enormous the population becomes.
Challenge this tempting claim: “A straight line on a log plot means the population adds a constant number.” Use a curved growth trace straightening on log paper to show what the model actually says.

Explain without the picture: What does a steeper straight line on an ln(population)-versus-time plot mean? Check your reasoning against: A larger continuous proportional growth rate k and a shorter doubling time.

visuals.title: A log scale turns ratios into distances
visuals.goal: A log axis folds each doubling into the same visual step, however enormous the population becomes.

lessons.objective: By the end you can relate generation-to-generation spread to R and the generation interval.

beats.text: Picture a transmission tree with two branches per node.
In a fixed-generation toy model with 10 initial infections and R=2, how many new infections occur in generation 3?
In a simple generation model, each infected person produces R further infections on average. Early growth can be approximated by I(g)=I0 R^g when conditions remain stable.
80 new infections: 10 × 2^3; this is not the cumulative total. Follow one branch of transmission and then imagine the same branching rule repeated at every tip.
Challenge this tempting claim: “R0 is a fixed property of a pathogen independent of population and context.” Use generation clocks beneath branching clusters to show what the model actually says.

Explain without the picture: How do R0 and the effective reproduction number Re differ? Check your reasoning against: R0 describes spread in a wholly susceptible population under specified conditions; Re reflects current susceptibility and interventions.

visuals.title: Epidemics as branching generations
visuals.goal: Follow one branch of transmission and then imagine the same branching rule repeated at every tip.

lessons.objective: By the end you can explain why resource feedback bends exponential growth into an S-curve.

beats.text: Picture a bottle filling while food icons disappear.
For logistic growth with K=1000, by what factor does the proportional rate differ from k at N=900?
The logistic model dN/dt=kN(1-N/K) slows growth near carrying capacity K. It approximates resource feedback rather than allowing exponential growth forever.
It is multiplied by 1−900/1000=0.1. The crowd still makes new members, but every new member also takes away a little of the room left to grow.
Challenge this tempting claim: “A carrying capacity forces an abrupt universal stop at a fixed time.” Use an s-curve approaching a dashed capacity line to show what the model actually says.
Explain without the picture: At what positive population is the absolute logistic growth rate largest when k>0? Check your reasoning against: N=K/2, where N(1−N/K) is maximal.

visuals.title: Resources bend the curve
visuals.goal: The crowd still makes new members, but every new member also takes away a little of the room left to grow.

lessons.objective: By the end you can calculate remaining fractions after several half-lives.

beats.text: Picture a pile shrinking from 80 to 40 to 20.
An ideal exponentially decaying sample starts at 80 mg with a 6-hour half-life. What remains after 18 hours?
Exponential decay removes a constant fraction in equal time intervals. For N=N0 exp(-λt), half-life is ln(2)/λ.
10 mg: three half-lives leave 80/8. Rewind a doubling story and each equal tick removes half of whatever remains, not half of the original pile.
Challenge this tempting claim: “A half-life means all material is gone after two half-lives.” Use independent glowing atoms switching off at random times to show what the model actually says.
Explain without the picture: How is half-life related to the positive decay constant λ? Check your reasoning against: T_half = ln(2)/λ.

visuals.title: Decay uses the same machinery
visuals.goal: Rewind a doubling story and each equal tick removes half of whatever remains, not half of the original pile.

lessons.objective: By the end you can identify when a growth extrapolation has lost its mechanistic justification.

beats.text: Picture a forecast cone widening beyond observed dots.
A culture doubles every hour for 3 hours, then stops dividing for lack of nutrients. Starting at 100, what is its final count in this idealization?
Exponential models are useful over intervals where proportional rates remain roughly stable. Changes in resources, behavior, or mechanisms can change the rate and invalidate extrapolation.
800; extending the earlier exponential beyond hour 3 would be incorrect. A formula is a local story about a mechanism, and its ending changes when the mechanism changes.
Challenge this tempting claim: “An excellent fit to early data guarantees indefinite exponential growth.” Use a growth engine with a changing rate dial to show what the model actually says.

Explain without the picture: What assumption should you check before extrapolating an exponential fit? Check your reasoning against: That the proportional growth mechanism and rate remain approximately stable over the forecast interval.

visuals.title: Know when the model stops working
visuals.goal: A formula is a local story about a mechanism, and its ending changes when the mechanism changes.
